scenes.heading: Homeostasis
scenes.sub: How your body stays steady at the beach or in the snow
scenes.say: Your body temperature stays close to thirty-seven degrees, whether you're at the beach or in the snow. How does your body keep things so steady? It's called homeostasis.
scenes.caption: Your body temperature stays close to 37 °C, whether you're at the beach or in the snow. How does your body keep things so steady? It's called homeostasis.

scenes.heading: The stimulus–response model
steps: Control centre: compares to set point
scenes.say: Every homeostasis mechanism follows the same model. A stimulus is a change. A receptor detects it. The control centre compares it with the set point. An effector, a muscle or gland, carries out the response. Remember: Silly Rabbits Can Eat Rice.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cruise control speeds up on a hill, then eases off at 100
scenes.science: Negative feedback reverses a change, then switches off
scenes.breaks: The body often uses several effectors at once, and values wobble within a tolerance range.
scenes.say: Think of cruise control set to one hundred. Going uphill, the car slows. A sensor detects it, the computer compares it with one hundred, and the engine adds power. Once it's back to one hundred, the extra power eases off. That's negative feedback. But your body often uses several effectors at once.
scenes.caption: Think of cruise control set to 100 km/h. Going uphill, the car slows. A sensor detects it, the computer compares it with 100, and the engine adds power. Once it's back to 100, the extra power eases off. That's negative feedback. But your body often uses several effectors at once.

scenes.heading: Controlling temperature
scenes.say: The hypothalamus is the control centre for temperature. When you're too hot, skin arterioles widen, called vasodilation, and you sweat more. When you're too cold, they narrow, called vasoconstriction, and you shiver. Remember, vessels widen, they don't move.

scenes.heading: Controlling blood glucose
scenes.say: Blood glucose is controlled by the pancreas. When it's high, beta cells release insulin. Cells take in glucose and store it as glycogen. When it's low, alpha cells release glucagon, and the liver breaks glycogen back down. Glucagon when glucose is gone. They're antagonistic hormones.

scenes.heading: Water balance and ADH
points: ADH released from the posterior pituitary
More water reabsorbed: less, darker urine
scenes.say: If your blood gets too concentrated, the hypothalamus detects it. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary. It makes collecting duct cells add more aquaporins, so more water moves back into the blood by osmosis. You make less, more concentrated urine. Anti-diuretic means anti-wee!

points: Insulin lowers glucose; glucagon raises it
ADH saves water in the kidneys
scenes.say: Quick recap. Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response. Negative feedback reverses a change, then switches off. Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it. And ADH helps your kidneys save water. Now try the practice questions!
